extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students and instructors in probability theory and mathematical statistics
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material about central limit theorems, weak convergence, and characteristic functions: definitions, equivalences, key theorems, and technical lemmas used to prove CLTs. Intended as course reading and reference for proofs and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: De Moivre-Laplace Theorem (Theorem 3.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a < b then as m → ∞, P(a ≤ S_m/√m ≤ b) → ∫_a^b (2π)^{-1/2} e^{-x^2/2} dx.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a special case of the central limit theorem. The restriction to even integers can be removed noting S_{2n+1} = S_{2n} ± 1. The theorem is used to approximate binomial/symmetric random-walk probabilities by the standard normal distribution; details are omitted as it is subsumed by the general CLT in Section 3.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of weak convergence (Fn ⇒ F)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of distribution functions Fn is said to converge weakly to F (written Fn ⇒ F) if Fn(y) → F(y) for all y that are continuity points of F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convergence at continuity points suffices because distribution functions are right-continuous and have at most countably many discontinuities. This definition underpins the various equivalent formulations and theorems in the section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence in distribution (Xn ⇒ X)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of random variables Xn is said to converge in distribution (weakly) to X∞ (written Xn ⇒ X∞) if their distribution functions Fn(x)=P(Xn ≤ x) converge weakly to the distribution function of X∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used interchangeably with weak convergence of distribution functions; examples illustrate phenomena such as convergence failing at discontinuities and scaling limits (e.g., rare events and exponential limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheffé's Theorem (total variation from pointwise density convergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fn (densities) converge pointwise to f∞ then for all Borel sets B, ∫_B fn(x) dx − ∫_B f∞(x) dx → 0; equivalently total variation norm ||µn − µ∞|| → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a convergence stronger than weak convergence. The proof uses dominated convergence and the fact fn ≥ 0 with integral 1. A counterexample (point masses moving to 0) shows weak convergence need not imply total-variation convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skorokhod representation (Theorem 3.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Fn ⇒ F∞ then there exist random variables Yn (on a common probability space) with distributions Fn such that Yn → Y∞ almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructed via quantile functions on (0,1): Yn(x)=sup{y: Fn(y) < x}. This representation is useful to convert weak convergence statements into almost-sure convergence statements for proving further properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization via bounded continuous functions (Theorem 3.2.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Xn ⇒ X∞ if and only if for every bounded continuous function g we have E g(Xn) → E g(X∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The forward direction follows from Skorokhod representation and bounded convergence. The converse is proved by approximating indicators of half-lines with bounded continuous functions gx,ε; the proof shows how to recover pointwise distribution convergence at continuity points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous mapping theorem (Theorem 3.2.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn ⇒ X∞ and g is measurable with discontinuity set Dg, and P(X∞ ∈ Dg) = 0, then g(Xn) ⇒ g(X∞). If g is bounded then also E g(Xn) → E g(X∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dg is a Borel set. The proof uses the Skorokhod representation: if Yn =d Xn and Yn → Y∞ a.s., then continuity of g at the limit point gives g(Yn) → g(Y∞) a.s., and bounded convergence yields convergence of expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portmanteau theorem / equivalent formulations (Theorem 3.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: The following are equivalent to Xn ⇒ X∞: (ii) for all open sets G, lim inf P(Xn ∈ G) ≥ P(X∞ ∈ G); (iii) for all closed sets K, lim sup P(Xn ∈ K) ≤ P(X∞ ∈ K); (iv) for Borel A with P(X∞ ∈ ∂A)=0, P(Xn ∈ A) → P(X∞ ∈ A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for proving weak convergence via topological set criteria. The text includes a mnemonic and sketch linking the inequalities and shows how (ii)-(iv) imply (i) by testing with half-lines at continuity points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helly's selection theorem (Theorem 3.2.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every sequence Fn of distribution functions there is a subsequence Fn(k) and a right-continuous nondecreasing function F so that Fn(k)(y) → F(y) at all continuity points y of F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The limit F may not be a distribution function because mass can escape to ±∞ (vague convergence). The diagonal argument using rationals is given; F is obtained via an infimum over rational limits. This result motivates the notion of tightness to prevent loss of mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tightness criterion and equivalence for probability limits (Theorem 3.2.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every subsequential limit of Fn is a distribution function of a probability measure iff the sequence Fn is tight, i.e., for all ε>0 there exists M(ε) with lim sup_{n→∞} [1 − Fn(M) + Fn(−M)] ≤ ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If tightness holds, any vague subsequential limit has total mass 1; conversely non-tightness provides a subsequence losing at least ε mass to ±∞. Tightness is the necessary and sufficient condition to ensure no mass is lost in Helly's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient condition for tightness via moment-like integrals (Theorem 3.2.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exists φ ≥ 0 with φ(x) → ∞ as |x| → ∞ and sup_n ∫ φ(x) dFn(x) < ∞ then {Fn} is tight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: 1 − Fn(M) + Fn(−M) ≤ C / inf_{|x|≥M} φ(x). This is a common way to prove tightness by controlling tail integrals (e.g., moment bounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential compactness criterion (Theorem 3.2.15)
rubrics_metrics.description: If every subsequence of Xn has a further subsequence that converges to X, then Xn ⇒ X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows because convergence comes from a metric for distribution convergence; the theorem is referenced and used later in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and basic properties of characteristic functions (Theorem 3.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a random variable X define ϕ(t)=E e^{itX} = E cos(tX) + i E sin(tX). Properties: (a) ϕ(0)=1; (b) ϕ(−t)=ϕ(t) (real/odd-even relations); (c) |ϕ(t)| ≤ 1; (d) ϕ is uniformly continuous on ℝ; (e) ϕ_{aX+b}(t) = e^{itb} ϕ(a t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use basic calculus and dominated convergence. These properties are the starting point for algebraic manipulation of ch.f.'s and for continuity arguments used in weak convergence proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product property for independent sums (Theorem 3.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X1 and X2 are independent with ch.f.'s ϕ1 and ϕ2, then the ch.f. of X1 + X2 is ϕ1(t) ϕ2(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follows from independence: E[e^{it(X1+X2)}] = E[e^{itX1}] E[e^{itX2}]. Used to compute ch.f.'s of sums and to derive distributional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion formula (Theorem 3.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ(t)=∫ e^{itx} µ(dx) and a < b then (2π)^{-1} lim_{T→∞} ∫_{-T}^T (e^{-ita} − e^{-itb})/(it) ϕ(t) dt = µ(a,b) + 1/2 µ({a,b}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence of the limit is part of the conclusion. The proof rewrites the kernel as ∫_a^b e^{−ity} dy and uses Riemann integrals and the bounded convergence theorem. Remark: the integral need not converge absolutely (e.g., δ_0 gives (2 sin t)/t integrand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrable characteristic functions imply bounded continuous density (Theorem 3.3.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∫_{−∞}^∞ |ϕ(t)| dt < ∞ then µ has a bounded continuous density f(y) = (1/2π) ∫ e^{-ity} ϕ(t) dt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute integrability of ϕ makes the inversion formula absolutely convergent; yields no point masses and continuity of f by dominated convergence. This ties decay of ϕ at ∞ to smoothness of µ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity theorem for characteristic functions (Theorem 3.3.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) If µn ⇒ µ∞ then ϕn(t) → ϕ∞(t) for all t. (ii) If ϕn(t) → ϕ(t) pointwise and ϕ is continuous at 0, then the sequence µn is tight and µn ⇒ µ (the measure with ch.f. ϕ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (ii) requires continuity at 0 (counterexample: normals with variance → ∞, which give pointwise limit 0 for t≠0 but do not converge weakly). The proof shows how integrals of 1 − ϕn over small intervals control tails and yield tightness, then subsequence arguments give full convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequality relating ϕ behavior near 0 to tail mass (used in proof of 3.3.17)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because |sin x| ≤ |x| and |sin ux| ≤ 1, discarding a small central integral yields a lower bound in terms of tail mass. Letting u→0 and using pointwise convergence of ϕn gives tightness. This inequality is a key technical link between characteristic function smoothness at 0 and tightness of the measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moments imply differentiability of characteristic function (Theorem 3.3.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∫ |x|^n µ(dx) < ∞ then the characteristic function ϕ has a continuous derivative of order n given by ϕ^{(n)}(t) = ∫ (i x)^n e^{itx} µ(dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiation under the integral is justified by dominated convergence. Consequently, E|X|^n < ∞ implies ϕ is n-times differentiable at 0 and ϕ^{(n)}(0) = E (iX)^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor remainder bound for e^{ix} (Lemma 3.3.19)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two bounds are provided: the usual small-x bound (n+1 power) and a better large-|x| bound (order n). The lemma is applied to control errors in characteristic-function Taylor expansions without assuming higher moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-moment Taylor expansion of ϕ (Theorem 3.3.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E|X|^2 < ∞ then ϕ(t) = 1 + i t E X − (t^2/2) E(X^2) + o(t^2) as t → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The error term is bounded by t^2 E( |t| |X|^3 ∧ 2 |X|^2 ); using dominated convergence yields o(t^2). This result is obtained without assuming a finite third moment by using the min-type remainder estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-derivative criterion implies finite second moment (Theorem 3.3.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim sup_{h↓0} [ϕ(h) − 2ϕ(0) + ϕ(−h)]/h^2 > −∞ then E|X|^2 < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses the identity (e^{ihx} − 2 + e^{-ihx})/h^2 = −2 (1 − cos(hx))/h^2 ≤ 0 and Fatou's lemma to pass to x^2 integrability. This gives a converse-type result linking smoothness of ϕ at 0 to finiteness of variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lévy metric and Ky Fan metric (Exercises 3.2.6–3.2.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lévy metric: ρ(F,G)=inf{ε: F(x−ε)−ε ≤ G(x) ≤ F(x+ε)+ε for all x} metrizes distribution convergence. Ky Fan metric on random variables: α(X,Y)=inf{ε: P(|X−Y|>ε) ≤ ε}. Relations: convergence in Ky Fan implies convergence in Lévy (ρ ≤ α) and metrics provide quantitative control of distributional convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics are used to show convergence in distribution comes from a metric and to relate probabilistic closeness of random variables to distributional closeness. Exercises give further inequalities between α and other metrics (e.g., β).
